criterion_scores.reasoning: The core new logic (runtime_ledgers.py + its wiring into check-refs.sh and build_graph.py) does satisfy the acceptance examples named in decision 5 (substrate.py and identity_probe.py both go from N missing to 0, the SessionStart check drops substrate-gate-failures.jsonl) — verified by running the actual scripts. But the same mechanism has a demonstrated, reproducible defect: it recognizes `.claude/artifacts/read-only.jsonl` and `.claude/artifacts/overwritten.jsonl` as legitimate runtime ledgers purely because runtime_ledgers.py's own selftest fixture text (in the file it scans, since it lives under one of WRITER_DIRS) satisfies its append-detection heuristic — directly contradicting numbered decisions 1 and 4 on precisely the scenario the diff itself set out to guarantee ('a ledger that is only ever read' / 'typo... still flags'). This is a code-contradicts-a-numbered-spec-decision defect (line 144), capping correctness per the rubric's fail anchor.

All required parts are present: check-refs.sh modified, runtime_ledgers.py built with --list/--check/--selftest, build_graph.py updated and given its own integration selftest (selftest_runtime_ledgers, confirmed it actually exercises the shell script against a live missing ledger + a typo, not skipped in this run). No TODO stubs. But test coverage is incomplete exactly where it mattered: the live-repo assertions (line 167) check only that true positives are recognized, never that the selftest's own negative-control names are absent from the live scan — the gap that let the correctness defect ship undetected by '12/12 pass'. Also the WRITER_DIRS scope (line 106) quietly narrows decision 1's 'some tracked script in the repo' to two directories, undisclosed.

Correct file placement (.claude/hooks/runtime_ledgers.py alongside check-refs.sh; executable bit set, mode 100755), proper shebang, ADR-8 D2 'one rule, one implementation, not two copies kept in sync by a comment' genuinely achieved — both tools delegate to the same module rather than duplicating logic. Comments correctly cite YED-227 and ADR-8. One cosmetic slip: the shell case-pattern (line 24) is glob-permissive of nested subdirectory paths in a way the python LEDGER_REF_RE is not, so the header's claim the extraction rules are 'shared VERBATIM' is not literally true for this new gate (though it causes no live bug given the downstream exact-match).

Lean, single-purpose fix; no over-engineering, no duplicated state beyond the necessary shared module, no tombstoned decision resurrected, no hardcoded secrets, no fabricated numbers. But the chosen implementation pattern — full-text regex scanning of every tracked file in the tool's own home directory, with no self-exclusion — is a foreseeable self-poisoning hazard, and the file is visibly aware of a sibling self-reference risk (the concatenation trick documented in its own selftest comment, guarding against check-refs.sh's grep) yet did not extend that same care to its own heuristic, which is exactly where the failure (defect 1) occurred.

Comments are clear and the WHY docstring is genuinely useful, explaining the append-vs-read distinction and one known limitation (co-occurrence, not dataflow, within a single real writer file). But the selftest's reported '12/12 pass' (line 173) overstates what is actually proven: it validates the heuristic only against an isolated, hand-built text dict, and validates the LIVE repo scan only for presence of true positives, never for absence of its own negative controls — so it reports full confidence on a guarantee (decision 4's 'read-only... still flags') that is demonstrably false on the deployed code path. This is the rubric's diagnostics fail anchor: 'a reported count ... overstates what's proven.'

defects.issue: runtime_ledgers.py's own selftest fixture text leaks into the LIVE `runtime_ledger_names()` used by check-refs.sh and build_graph.py, because runtime_ledgers.py lives under `.claude/hooks/` (one of WRITER_DIRS, line 89) and `tracked_writer_texts()` (line 106) scans every tracked .py/.sh file there with no self-exclusion. The module's own source text contains an append-mode-shaped substring (`open(LOG, "a", ...)` inside the fixture at line ~142) and lines mentioning "artifacts" plus a `.jsonl` name (this line, and the 'writer_w.py'/'overwritten.jsonl' fixture at line 146) — so `APPEND_RE.search(text)` on the whole file matches, and `NAME_RE` sweeps up the DELIBERATE NEGATIVE-CONTROL names the selftest chose to prove should NOT be recognized. Reproduced live in the worktree: `python3 .claude/hooks/runtime_ledgers.py --check .claude/artifacts/read-only.jsonl .claude/artifacts/overwritten.jsonl` prints BOTH as recognized runtime ledgers, and `check-refs.sh` on a fresh temp artifact referencing `.claude/artifacts/read-only.jsonl` (a name with no real writer anywhere in the repo — confirmed via `git grep`) silently skips it as a 'runtime ledger'. This directly contradicts numbered decision 1 ('Anything else still flags, including ... a ledger that is only ever read') and decision 4 ('read-only reference to a missing file still flags') on the exact scenario the diff's own selftest names as a must-reject case — the guarantee holds only in the isolated `ledgers_from_texts(texts)` unit test, not on the deployed code path.

The live-repo portion of the selftest (the `for must in (...)` loop at line 167) only asserts that the four true-positive ledger names ARE recognized; it never asserts that the selftest's own negative-control names (`read-only.jsonl`, `overwritten.jsonl`, or the bare `gate-failures.jsonl`, none of which have any real writer in the repo per `git grep`) are ABSENT from the live `runtime_ledger_names()` cache. So the exact self-poisoning regression above runs silently through to '12/12 pass' with zero signal — the reported count overstates what the test actually proves about the deployed behaviour, and the module docstring's 'KNOWN LIMITATION' section (documented only for a different case: a real writer file that also merely reads an unrelated ledger) does not disclose this more severe self-referential failure mode.

The chosen mechanism — regex-scanning the raw text of every tracked file in the very directory the tool itself lives in, with no exclusion of its own filename — is a foreseeable self-poisoning hazard. The file is otherwise visibly careful about a DIFFERENT self-reference trap (the selftest's own comment, a few lines below the fixtures, explains why fixture paths are built by string concatenation so they "never appear as literal `.claude/...` tokens ... a literal would become a real dangling reference in the system graph") but that defense only protects against check-refs.sh's plain grep; it does nothing against ledgers_from_texts' looser, ANY-line, any-jsonl-name sweep, which is exactly what leaked the negative-control names (defect 1).

Decision 1 says a ledger is exempted when 'some tracked script in the repo' appends to it (unrestricted location), but the implementation only ever searches WRITER_DIRS = .claude/scripts and .claude/hooks. Nothing in the diff states this as a deliberate scoping choice. Currently harmless (a repo-wide `git grep` for append-mode writers to any `.claude/artifacts/*.jsonl` found none outside those two directories), but it is a narrower guarantee than the spec's literal wording and is undisclosed.

check-refs.sh's shell case-pattern uses `*` glob matching, which (unlike a strict path-segment match) also matches a nested subdirectory such as `.claude/artifacts/sub/x.jsonl` — looser than runtime_ledgers.py's anchored `LEDGER_REF_RE` (`^(?:\./)?\.claude/artifacts/([A-Za-z0-9._-]+\.jsonl)$`), which forbids any `/` in the captured name. ADR-8 D2 / the file header say the extraction rules are 'shared VERBATIM' between the two tools; this specific gate is not actually the same rule expressed twice, it just happens to converge because the subsequent exact-string match against `--list` output re-imposes the strict boundary. No live bug (verified: a subdirectory path falls through to the normal checked/missing accounting), but it's a maintenance trap if either side changes independently.
